t: Match Substring After Replacement — Mapping Table plus Scan
o: Character old can play the role of new if old == new or (old, new) appears in mappings (replacements chain through distinct characters only once, but since each sub character is replaced at most once and mappings entries are independent, a direct lookup table suffices). Build a 128x128 boolean table, then try every alignment of sub in s and check all positions with the table. Sizes (5000 x 5000 = 25M comparisons) pass easily in optimized languages; in Python, precompute per-character allowed sets to speed the inner loop.
k: Precompute a boolean compatibility matrix match[c1][c2] once.
Naive substring scanning with the matrix is O(|s| * |sub|) = 25M, acceptable.

a.i: match[c1][c2] is true when c1 can appear as c2 after zero or one replacement. Slide sub over s; a position matches if every pair passes the matrix.
s: Fill match[c][c]=true and match[old][new]=true from mappings.
For each start i in s, verify all j of sub via the matrix; return true on success.
Return false after all alignments fail.
a.t: O(|s| * |sub|) — up to 25 million constant-time character checks.

a.n: Approach 2: Position Filtering by Rare Character
a.i: Pick the sub position whose allowed-source set is smallest; candidate alignments of s must place one of those characters there. Bucket indices of s by character, intersect candidate sets across positions, and verify survivors. This prunes aggressively in practice, though worst-case complexity is unchanged.
s: For each sub position j, compute set S_j of characters c with match[c][sub[j]].
Candidates = indices of s whose character is in S_j0 for the smallest S_j0.
Filter candidates against remaining positions; return true if any survive.
a.t: Worst case O(|s| * |sub|), typically far faster due to pruning.

w: The matrix + scan is the interview answer; mention KMP-style failure functions exist but are unnecessary at these sizes. Pitfall: replacements are one-way ('o'->'0' does not allow '0'->'o') and each sub character is replaced at most once, so no transitive chaining is needed. Follow-up: allow chained mappings — then compute transitive closure per character.
